newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices resume surge, copper also firm.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices resume surge, copper also firm.

text.p: Coffee prices surged again on Wednesday after coffee-exporting countries agreed to extend an agreement to limit their exports for another 12 months despite recent soaring world prices.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for July delivery closed 12.85 cents a pound higher 253.10 cents.

The market rose early on weather forecasts for cold weather moving into Brazil later this week. No frost is expected yet in the number one producer's coffee regions, but traders remain jittery about that prospect as winter begins.

Prices then shot higher when Association of Coffee Producing Countries at a meeting in London agreed to keep their scheme of coffee export quotas until July 1998 and limit annual shipments by the 14 members to 52.75 million 132-pound bags of coffee, unchanged from the current year.

"Talk the ACPC was loosening quotas was part of the bearish news affecting the market over the last few days," said Allendale analyst Jim Cordier. "The fact they're not going to follow through on that is bullish."
Coffee prices had fallen for three consecutive days after hitting a 20-year high of 280 cents a pound.
"The market is coming back to levels seen early in the week," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "It had failed because people feared the sudden release of coffee hiding in some warehouse."

Low inventory levels in both consuming and producing countries, combined with smaller crops in many Latin America nations and projections for a reduced crop in Brazil next season, have been behind coffee's five-month rally.

Copper prices also continued to rise. Copper for July delivery at COMEX in New York ended 0.35 cent a pound higher at 118.20 cents, touching a new life-of-contract high during the day and remaining at the highest levels seen in a year.

"The market looks close to being overbought, but it does certainly appear there is still considerable upside potential," said John Gross of the Copper Journal, who pointed to declines in warehouses stocks for both COMEX and the London Metal Exchange as examples of strong commercial demand.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, prices for pork bellies closed with gains near the daily 3.00-cent a pound trading limit after a government report showed low stocks.
Pork bellies for July delivery closed 2.80 cents a pound higher at 93.35 cents.

The Agriculture Department said frozen pork belly stocks as of April 30 totalled 54.017 million pounds, less than 54.767 million reported on March 31 and below the 57.174 million pounds a year earlier. It marked only the second time frozen belly stockpiles dropped during April.
U.S. pork exports to Japan and other Asian nations have continued strong since Taiwan suspended pork exports in March due to an outbreak of disease in the island's hog herd.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices rose on reports of another incursion by Turkish forces across the Iraqi border into Kurdish rebel-held territory. Crude oil for July delivery rose 27 cents to end at $21.86 a barrel.

Crude oil prices have fluctuated sharply over the past several sessions, rising last week despite reports of increased U.S. oil inventories. But even with a bounce of about $2 a barrel since the start of May, crude is still about $5 a barrel lower since the start of the year, analysts said.
"I think crude is headed to $18 a barrel. We're swimming in the stuff," said A.G. Edwards analyst Bill O'Grady.
July delivery gasoline closed 0.56 cent a gallon higher at 64.87 cents and July heating oil up 0.01 cent a gallon at 57.68 cents.
